<!-- Lessons from the APL side quest, written 2026-09-15 for the next person who
     writes a sub-language in this tree. Every claim cites a numbered row of
     explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md (section 16 holds the sixty-three rows
     about the mechanism itself) and the probe that proves it; probe paths are
     relative to explorations/. This is not a manual and not a row list: the
     manual is ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Syntax.rats, and the
     rows are in the ledger. -->

# Extending Fortress's syntax: lessons from the APL ladder

Between 2026-09-11 and 2026-09-15 an APL was written as a sub-language of Fortress: a feasibility study (`apl-probes/REPORT.md`), six rungs of Stefan Kruger's "Learning APL" climbed chapter by chapter inside `apl⦇ … ⦈` (`apl/rung-1` … `apl/rung-6`), a port of a 25-line flat-style microGPT (`apl/microgpt/`), and then a rewrite of the calling convention for that one program (`apl/mg/`). The purpose was never APL: it was to find where the specification's syntax-extension mechanism and the library give out, and what exactly gives. This document is what a later DSL writer needs in the order they will meet it; the evidence is in the ledger's rows 179-287 and in the probe directories named beside each claim.

The one thing to know before starting: the mechanism runs, it carried a real language, and every wall it has is documented below, but the tooling around it is the worst in the tree, so plan the work as a sequence of small bisecting probes rather than as one grammar you debug at the end.

## Declaring a grammar and importing it

The form that is implemented is FOOL'09's `grammar … end`, declared inside an api; the specification's own normative form, `syntax OpenExpander Id CloseExpander = Expr`, is not implemented at all, and the word `syntax` is not even a declaration keyword (row 267, `apl-probes/b12_spec_syntax_form.fss`). Chapter 27 of the specification is a one-sentence stub pointing at the paper, so the only description of the live spelling in this tree is `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Syntax.rats`, 434 lines; read it first, because most of the shipped examples are written in a dead pre-`=>` spelling that fails to parse, and the build never runs them (row 268 — `SyntaxAbstractionJUTestAll.java:36` and `:39` glob the top directory only, and `build.xml:1260` hangs off `testNightly`, so the green suite says nothing about syntax abstraction either way).

A grammar may live only in an api, never in a component (row 269), so a sub-language is always three files: the grammar api, a stub component exporting it, and the component that uses it (`apl-probes/e30_aplg.fsi` + `e30_aplg.fss` + `e30_apl.fss`, and at scale `apl/base/AplSyntax.fsi` + `AplCore.fss`). They need not sit in one directory, but `FORTRESS_SOURCE_PATH` replaces the shipped default rather than extending it, and the default is four entries (row 190).

Three spellings cost a run each if you do not know them. An api that gives one of its own nonterminals an AST type must `import FortressAst.{...}`, or every annotation in it is undefined, with no diagnostic naming the missing import and nothing in the specification mentioning it (row 271, `gap-ledger-probes/apl-merge/f01_noast*`). A nonterminal may not be named with a word of two or more uppercase letters, because such a word is an operator and not an identifier — `WE` is rejected with a bare `Syntax Error` at the name, and the implementation's rule is looser than the specification's, accepting `AAA` (row 193, `NodeUtil.java:1460-1477`). And the expander's brackets are not privileged: `⦇` U+2987 and `⦈` U+2988 are simply unused anywhere in the parser, the operator table, the library or the specification, so they were free (row 277); any glyph run works that contains none of the macro language's special characters.

The tax is the edit-run loop. Two Rats! parser generations happen at run time, about forty seconds on a cold cache, so a JDK with `javac` on the classpath is a hard requirement for any program that uses a grammar (row 266). `fortress parse` checks the preparser and parser in about 0.6 s and is the only fast check available — but it always fails on a component that *uses* an expander, with an empty message, because it does not run the syntax-abstraction phase (row 191). So grammar apis can be checked quickly and using components cannot, which is why every rung of the ladder kept its probes as separate small components with their own grammars.

## What a gap can and cannot be

A gap is a pattern variable in a production, typed `Id`, `Expr`, or one of your own nonterminals, and it is the only way text from the use site reaches the expansion. An `Expr` gap is the workhorse and behaves well, with one large caveat about greed treated below. The `Id` gap is where the design gives out.

An `Id` gap works in exactly one position: spliced into a lambda parameter, where it binds an ordinary Fortress variable that later statements of the sub-language read under their own spelling and that host code in the same block reads as itself (row 201, `apl/v1-probes/q01_bind.fss`, `q06_block.fss`). It cannot be read as a variable reference anywhere — bare it dies in the template parser, and kept off an expression's first token it dies in the disambiguator, because `Transform.forVarRef` looks a `VarRef`'s id up in the hygiene environment instead of recurring into it, so a gap inside a `VarRef` is never substituted (rows 182, 202). It cannot stand left of `=` or `:=`, because the template parser reads that position with its `AssignLeft` production, where a gap's text arrives null (rows 186, 196); four spellings were tried across two rungs before the design moved. And it refuses `_`, so APL's throw-away name had to be given a real one (row 242).

Repetition works, with one legal use. A `*`- or `+`-bound gap splices into a template with `**`, but only into a list literal carrying an explicit static type — drop the `[\ZZ32\]` and the aggregate's element type is computed from the runtime class and the unification fails (row 272, row 20's mechanism met through an expansion). Used without the `**` splice, the same gap crashes the generated parser with a raw Java cast error and no Fortress diagnostic at all (row 273; `ComposingSyntaxDefTranslator.java:489-490` returns the raw Java list with its conversion commented out beneath). A bound `?` gap — a `Maybe`-typed optional — is `not supported now`, with twenty lines of implementation commented out under the throw (row 274, `:508-509`); that is why an elided axis in `m[1;]` needs a production of its own rather than an optional gap, and why a reduce slash cannot be made optional inside one production (rows 197, 180).

The last constraint is the deepest: a transformer is a template, not a computation. `case … of` in a transformer dispatches only on `Cons(h,t)` and `Empty` over a repetition-bound list, never on an AST constructor name, and asking what an `Expr` gap *is* gives `Unrecognized constructor name: IntLiteralExpr` (row 275; `TemplateVarRewriter.java:122-147` and `Transform.java:752-762`, with `// Nothing else implemented yet`). So the grammar can ask how many items a repetition matched and nothing else. Every decision that depends on a value belongs in the expansion, which is why the feasibility grammar carried each glyph to the expansion as a `String` and let two dispatchers in the using component do the work (row 282), and why the later bases expanded straight to typed calls.

## Hygiene, and the two ways a name can meet its binder

Hygiene is implemented, and it is exactly what forbids the obvious trick. A binder written as a literal identifier inside a template is gensymmed; the free name of another rule's template is not; so the two never meet, and a preamble written by one rule — `(fn (v, m) => (blk))(cell(), cell())` — leaves every reference template unbound (row 204, `apl/v1-probes/q08_cell.fss`, which fails with `Variable m is not defined.` reported at the grammar api's line 1). A name and its binder can therefore meet in only two ways: both come through a gap (row 201), or both come from the use site's own declarations (row 206).

The second of those is the mechanism everything here is built on: free identifiers inside a `<[ … ]>` template resolve at the use site, not in the grammar's api (row 270, `apl-probes/b05_hygiene.fss`). A grammar may name `aplDy`, `rows`, `gather`, `pow`, and the component that uses the grammar supplies them — so a grammar api never has to export an operator across an api boundary, which is the standing workaround for row 30. The host may also simply declare the sub-language's variables, and then both sides see every update across separate use sites (row 206).

The flip side is the error story, and it is bad. An unbound free name in a template is a static failure before anything runs, reported against the grammar api at line 1 column 2 (row 243); so is a type error inside an expansion (row 213); so is a missing overload reached through an expansion, which arrives as a host unification error against the same span (row 230). A use of the expander that matches no production is not reported as a syntax error at all — the bracketed text is left unparsed and the keyword before it is read as an ordinary identifier, `Variable apl is not defined` (row 229). A partial match does at least give a `Syntax Error` at a real column, though the column is the furthest-failure position and not the offending token (rows 242, 261). The paper this mechanism comes from requires errors at use sites to refer to the unexpanded program at use sites; this implementation does the opposite, and the practical consequence is that a sub-language of any size is debugged by bisection.

One positive to end on: a typed lambda written whole inside one template works and dispatches, because hygiene renames the binder and its references together, and the lambda then selects an arrow-typed overload exactly as a hand-written one does (row 285, `apl/probes-4b/y02_lambda.fss`; the negative control, a binder in one template and its reference in another, is `y04_split.fss`). A template can also assign, if the left of `:=` is a literal name of the template rather than a gap (row 205) — so the wall of rows 186 and 196 is the gap, not the assignment.

## The closed name sets, and why

Since a name cannot be read through a gap, a sub-language that wants `v` to mean the user's `v` must spell the name in the grammar: a character class of letters concatenated right-recursively into a `String`, which is how the shipped `Xml.fsi` builds its attribute names (row 194). The class must be letter-then-letter-or-digit, APL's own rule: a single class `[A:Za:z0:9]` is tried before a numeral and the `9` of `9 2 6` is read as a name.

And a terminal that is a valid identifier becomes a keyword of the *whole language*: it is made a `KeywordSymbol`, every keyword of a user grammar is added to `FORTRESS_KEYWORDS`, and `Id` then excludes it, so writing `v` as a terminal to recognise it makes `v` unreadable as a name everywhere, templates included (row 203; the bisection is `q04`/`q05`). Spelled as a character class, `[v]`, it is a `CharacterClassSymbol` and reserves nothing. The same fact prices the entry form: a bare `apl` keyword would reserve the word `apl` program-wide, while `apl⦇` is not a valid identifier and so is an ordinary token.

The consequence is a closed name set: one grammar alternative per name, sixty-five array names, twenty-six strand names and five function names by the last rung of the universal base, and 124 of the focused base's 197 alternatives. It is cheap to write and it has three costs worth knowing in advance. A name outside the set is a `Syntax Error` at the use site rather than a value error at run time. A strand rule over every name merges two names on consecutive lines into one strand, so rung 5 had to read a *third*, disjoint set for strand elements (row 253). And a name may carry a digit after a capital and an underscore, but the underscore's class must be written `` [`_] `` — a bare `[_]` is a Syntax Error at the character — and a name with an underscore must stand above its prefix in the set (row 257).

Names must also survive the host. Its keywords are unusable (`value`, `at`, `type`, `label`, `wrapped` and eighty-odd more, rows 8, 262), every name the using component imports is unusable as a local (`Variable rows is already declared`, row 262), and there is no shadowing anywhere in this language, across five kinds of name (rows 92, 147, 167, 168). On the lambda route a name can also be bound only once per block, since a second `←` is a nested lambda parameter of the same name (row 207). The way out of that one is to bind a *mutable value* rather than to rebind: the library's arrays are mutable through a `Vector`/`Matrix` parameter, so `v[3] ← ¯1` became an in-place put and every later assignment stopped being a rebinding (row 224).

## PEG greed, and where rule order decides

The generated parser is a Rats! PEG: ordered choice, no backtracking into a nonterminal for a shorter match. Every surprise in this section follows from that one sentence.

An undelimited `Expr` gap is greedy and swallows whatever host-known operator follows it: `⍎v ≡ 1 4⍴⍎v` parsed as one `EQV` application inside the first gap (row 183). Delimiters do not help, because the closing delimiter is not a barrier the gap can see: a rule `( a:AplE , b:AplE ) ⍴ r` never matches once the grammar also has a catenate rule, and only atom-typed gaps make it match (row 235). The rule this yields for separators is sharp and was learned twice: a host `Expr` gap may be followed only by a terminal that is *outside* the host's operator table, or by one of your own nonterminals — a rule `y⦇ a:Expr ⋄ b:Expr ⦈` never matches, because `⋄` is the host's DIAMOND operator, and `∘` behaves the same, while `⍤`, which is in no host table, separates cleanly (row 284, `apl/probes-4b/y01_named.fss`).

Inside an ordinary nonterminal, rule order decides: the first alternative that succeeds wins, so a specialised rule must stand above the general one it refines. A rule whose left argument is parenthesised must stand above the plain rule for the same glyph, or the atom rule's own `( … )` consumes the parenthesis first and the specialised rule is never reached — and the failure is not a syntax error but a *wrong parse* that reaches the library and surfaces as a missing overload against the grammar api (row 236). The folded reduction `+/l×r` must likewise stand above the plain `+/v` (row 287).

Between alternatives of one macro *bracket*, order does not decide at all: the closing bracket makes the parser backtrack across alternatives, so a shorter alternative placed above a longer one still lets the longer one match (row 287's positive half). Two more bracket facts cost a worker four false diagnoses between them: a use of the expander cannot be an operand of a juxtaposition — `("" apl⦇ 5 ⦈)` is `Variable apl is not defined`, while the same use as a function argument or a binding's right-hand side parses (row 239) — and nine uses of the expander in one expression do not parse where eight do (row 261).

What the PEG gives for free is worth saying too: APL's strand notation needs ordered choice and nothing else. `AplStrand` is right-recursive over the host's `LiteralExpr` and backtracks at the first glyph, so `2 3 ⍴ ⍳ 6` needs no lookahead predicate; and right-to-left evaluation falls out of the *shape* of the productions — a dyadic rule takes a strand on the left and the whole rest of the expression on the right — so the host's precedence simply does not apply inside the brackets (`apl-probes/REPORT.md` §E, row 282).

## Separators, line breaks and the host's operator table

Whitespace in a production is optional at the use site: a literal space between symbols and an explicit `SPACE` both translate to the host's optional-whitespace nonterminal `w` (row 179). That is what lets a book's examples be copied in verbatim. The converse is that nothing can *require* a space, and `#` after a symbol is the deletion of that optional `w`, not a way to demand one (row 212); its real uses are gluing a name's characters together and gluing a high minus to its digits.

Because `w` crosses line breaks, a line break does not separate two statements whenever the next line can extend the phrase above it. The ladder widened this four times: first by a numeral (row 228), then by any dyadic glyph (row 238), then by the operand of a dfn or a named function (row 241), and finally by two ordinary names (row 253). Three remedies exist, all used: an explicit separator terminal (`⋄`), a comment tail bounded by the end of the line — which needs `#` on *every* symbol of it, or the optional whitespace looks past the newline and the comment swallows the statements below (row 227) — and a non-consuming `AND NEWLINE` lookahead for a form that ends at the line (row 209). A form with no terminator at all parses and then silently runs on (row 210), which is why the shipped regex grammar's bracket-free shape is safe only because a regex is closed by its second slash.

A line break *inside* a production is the opposite of optional whitespace: it is a required line break at the use site, so a rule split across two lines never matches a use written on one, and a long production must be written on one long line however wide (row 244). The break before `=>` is a different position and is free.

Statements are available: `⋄` as an ordinary terminal separates them, and so does a line break written in the production, which becomes the host parser's own `br` — which means a `;` works in its place too (row 208).

The host's operator table is the other half of the design. APL's functional-symbol block U+2336-U+237A is not an operator character set, by specification as well as by implementation: the operator characters are enumerated in `appendices/operators.tex`, and the only U+23xx codepoints there are `⌈ ⌉ ⌊ ⌋`; adding a glyph means regenerating `Operators.java` from `operators.txt`, that is, changing the language (row 278). Inside a sub-grammar the same glyphs are ordinary terminals, and so is any character class over them, because a generated Rats! parser matches raw characters and never goes through the Fortress lexer (row 276). But the *shared* glyphs are usable at the ordinary level and should be: `× ÷ - + * ⊖ ⊂ ⊃ ≡ ≢ ∘` each take a prefix and an infix declaration, so APL's monadic/dyadic split is ordinary overloading (rows 216, 279); `≠ < > ≥ ∧ ∨` take infix declarations returning an array rather than a `Boolean` (rows 218, 233); `⌈ ⌊` are enclosers and can only be declared as bracketing operators with unparenthesised parameters (rows 216, 280); `,` takes neither fixity. So a glyph can be reached two ways, and the ladder used both: a real host operator where the table allows one, a terminal plus a template where it does not.

The macro language's own special characters — `space : ? # + * [ ] | _ { }` and the backtick — must be backtick-escaped in a *terminal*, though not inside a template (row 222), and `\` and `.` refuse the escape entirely, being plain items (row 250). The escape is also this mechanism's nastiest trap. The preparser reads a backtick as an opening quote wanting a closing one and rejects the api — unless an APL glyph stands above it, because the preparser cannot tokenise such a glyph, its token loop then stops, and the delimiter check is silently skipped from there on (row 181). The portable form of the same trick is a `**` above the escape, which is why the shipped `Regex.fsi`, which backtick-escapes nine characters, is accepted at all: it disables the checker on its own line 93 (row 211). Both rows are worth reading before writing a production that needs an escape.

## What a template can and cannot expand to

It can expand to a host operator application, prefix or infix, with the operator characters unescaped (row 222); to a call; to a typed lambda written whole (row 285); to an assignment to a literally named `var` (row 205); to a list literal with a `**` splice, if the literal carries a static type (row 272); and to a block of statements. It cannot expand to a binding or an assignment whose left side is a gap (rows 186, 196), and it cannot mention a name the use site does not have (rows 204, 243).

One silent failure is worth more than the rest of this section. A template that writes the host's caret drops its right operand without a word: `<[ (1.0 (l)) ^ (r) ]>` expands to `1.0 (l)`, so `apl⦇ 10*10 ⦈` evaluated to `10.0` and `apl⦇ 2*3 ⦈` to `2.0`, the causal mask came out `-10` instead of `-1E10`, and every loss of the model moved from the seventh digit — three runs before the cause was found (row 286, `apl/mg/checks/model_run.out.1`). Routed through a one-line glue function `pow(b: RR64, e: ZZ32): RR64 = b^e`, the same rule is exact. Nothing in six rungs had put a host infix operator other than `+ - × ÷` inside a template, which is why nothing caught it earlier. The rule for the next sub-language: no host caret in a template, and treat any other host operator in a template as unproven until a probe prints its value.

## Function values, the frame stack, and why it was replaced

APL's direct functions take implicit arguments `⍺` and `⍵` and recur implicitly through `∇`. None of those can be a binder written by a template, because hygiene renames a template's own binder and the reference written by another rule never meets it (row 204), and the host refuses a nested lambda that re-declares an enclosing name (row 207). So the universal base answered with a frame stack: every APL function value, glyphs included, is a zero-parameter lambda over one mutable stack of frames; `aplCall(f, ⍺, ⍵)` pushes, calls `f()`, and pops; `⍺ ⍵ ∇` are frame reads; and APL's own rule that `⍺ ⍵` are never inherited comes for free (row 245). It is the only shape that survives nesting, and it carried two whole chapters of the book, including dops-in-waiting and glyphs as first-class values (row 234).

It cost three things. Everything on that route is untyped — `() -> Any` in and `Object` out — because an overloaded family whose declared *result* type is `Any` does not dispatch at all, however exactly the parameters match (row 240), leaving `Object` as the only declarable result and one contested row about whether the interpreter should accept a tuple declared that way (row 258). It is slow where the call is per element: 3.5× a direct `+` on scalars and nothing measurable on 100-element vectors (row 245), but 3.8× on a real 16×16 product, which pays 8192 frame pushes (row 256). And it is unsafe under the language's own implicit parallelism: the elements of a tuple expression are evaluated in parallel in separate implicit threads, so `¨` over a strand of three arrays pushed three frames onto one stack and the model died at pool size 4 (row 265). The base sequences the two sites it controls, and the limit stands everywhere else the host may evaluate two calls in parallel.

The focused base dropped the whole mechanism for the one program that mattered. Its single principle is that no function value crosses a rule boundary untyped: a function appears in APL text only as a *name*, which resolves at the use site to a typed host declaration (rows 270, 285) and picks its overload by arrow type (row 171), or as a derived function that one rule expands whole, so hygiene's renaming is consistent within it. That removed the `Any`, the `Object`, the frame pushes and the race together, and the sub-language then cost what the hand-written program costs at both pool sizes (`apl/mg/REPORT.md`). What was given up is real: dfn bodies, `⍺ ⍵ ∇`, guards, dops, glyphs as values — the subject of two of the six rungs.

The lesson generalises. If your sub-language needs user-written functions with implicit arguments, the frame stack is the shape that works; expect it to be untyped, about 3.5× per call, and to need every parallel-evaluated group sequenced by hand. If the programs are known in advance, spend the rules on them instead and keep everything typed.

## Rank in the type

The first APL library carried the rank as run-time data: one `value object AplArr(shape, data)` with every primitive dispatching on a string. It worked, and it was retired after two rungs because it was an interpreter nested inside the interpreter and taught nothing about Fortress (`apl/README.md`; its probes survive as `apl/v1-probes/` because the mechanism rows cite them).

The replacement put the rank in the type: a scalar is an `RR64`, a vector a `Vector[\RR64,s\]`, a matrix a `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]`, a rank-3 array an `Array3` (row 246). That buys a great deal from the host. Rank overloading works and the `nat` is inferred from a runtime-built array (row 214); overloading on the *index's* rank works too, so "a scalar index lowers the rank, a vector index keeps it" is dispatch and never a shape test (row 225); a six-line view object over a runtime-sized matrix is a real `Vector` where the library's own slice is not (rows 226, 55); `requires` contracts on the declarations fire through a macro expansion as catchable violations, so APL's LENGTH, INDEX and DOMAIN ERROR are contracts (rows 220, 231); a library array is already a full generator, with `|v|`, comprehensions, `SUM` and `BIG MAX` and no mix-in at all (row 221); and the shipped `opr DOT` is already APL's inner product in all four rank pairs (row 254).

It costs one declaration per rank combination — thirty-six for one chapter's bracket algebra (row 225) — and it has one hard edge: the single primitive whose result rank is a run-time value, dyadic `⍴` with a computed left argument, cannot be fixed in the grammar, and reinstating it means a sum type over the ranks plus a `typecase` at the head of every primitive, that is, re-entering the whole design through one glyph (row 223). An element type outside the numeric tower is a second edge: a `Char` array cannot join a rank-overloaded family beside an `RR64` one, because `Vector` demands `T extends Number` and the two are both `Rank1` with nothing excluding between them (row 219), so every character primitive is a separate name family.

The trade, stated once: rank in the type buys the host's dispatch, contracts, generators and parallelism; rank as data buys a computed rank and nested values. The programs in this tree wanted the first, and the measurements say the first is also the fast one.

## The cost facts

A direct grammar rule that reaches a typed library entry costs 3.8× less than the same function routed through the general call, measured on the workload these programs are made of: 12.97 s against 49.32 s for 200 products of 16×16 matrices (row 256). That single number is the argument for the direct rules of rungs 1, 3, 5 and 6, and for the focused base as a whole. One frame push is 3.5× a direct `+` on scalars and unmeasurable on 100-element vectors (row 245): the cost appears exactly where the call is per element.

A rule should delegate rather than loop: the shipped `DOT` is 1.46× a hand-written triple loop in the same library (row 256), so `+.×` is one line per rank pair with a contract above it, not a loop.

Parser generation is the fixed tax: two Rats! generations at run time per program, about forty seconds cold (row 266), and no fast check for a component that uses an expander (row 191). Budget for it, keep probes small, and bisect.

The end-to-end number is the one that settles the approach. The focused base expresses 19 of the program's 25 Dyalog lines as APL text over an existing Fortress vocabulary, and its forward pass agrees with the hand-written program intermediate by intermediate to 0.0, its 40 checks pass at both pool sizes with identical values, and its cost is the hand-written program's: 439 s against 528 s and 444 s at pool size 1, 254 s against 263 s at pool size 4 (`apl/mg/REPORT.md`). The universal base's 1.12× and 1.49× on the same checks were the frame stack and its sequential general route. A sub-language's expansion cannot be better than the vocabulary it expands to — and it need not be worse.

## The walls

**Nested arrays.** The flat carrier's wall is the element type: no element can be an array, and a boxed element is a new *representation* rather than a new function, so one trait and two variants replace one carrier and all sixty-five top-level functions are typed in the old one (row 199; the skeleton runs, so the price is measured and not argued). The ladder's answer was to avoid nesting entirely: a strand of arrays became a Fortress tuple, which dispatches on arity, may be an overloaded family's result type, holds values of three different ranks, and binds through a lambda of that many parameters (row 252). A tuple is not an array, so this works only where the nesting is one level and known — which is where it was.

**Implicit arguments.** `⍺ ⍵ ∇` cannot be binders written by a template (rows 204, 207); either a frame stack with everything that implies, or no user-written functions inside the sub-language. There is no third answer in this implementation.

**Characters.** A `Char` array cannot join the rank-overloaded family (row 219), so characters cost a parallel set of names for every primitive; nine of one chapter's examples and the whole of the character material stayed out of scope for this reason. A string literal has no `\u` escape either, so a glyph must stand in the source — which works, the tree being read as UTF-8 (row 200).

**And the diagnostics.** Every static error inside an expansion points at the grammar api's line 1 (rows 213, 230, 243), a use that matches nothing is not reported as a syntax error at all (row 229), and a reported column is a furthest-failure position rather than the offending token (rows 242, 261). No design choice avoids this; only small components and bisection do.

## Where the record is thin, or disagrees with itself

The ledger and the ladder's reports agree about the mechanism, and where they differed the ledger's row carries the correction rather than the report: rung 2b concluded that a sub-language comment may only follow the *last* statement of a block, which is true only of a tail spelled `NOT ⦈ _` and is corrected by row 227; and `apl/base/AplCore.fss`'s own header says a top-level `opr` declared in an api does not reach an importing component, which row 215 falsifies — row 30 is about library generic code failing to see a user operator, not about a user call site. Four APL rows cited the feasibility study's table as though it had been merged before it was; it is now rows 266-283. One count is off in the review that classified the rows: it prices the syntax-extension worklist item at twenty rows and its own list names twenty-one.

Two thin places are worth naming. Nothing in any of this was run on the bytecode-compiler path — every row is the walk interpreter — and the syntax-abstraction tests are not in the green suite at all (row 268), so the suite says nothing about the mechanism either way. And the one contested claim in this area is row 258's type half: a tuple returned as a declared `Object` result, which the specification does not admit and the walk interpreter accepts.

The paper the rows argue with (`research/extracts/growing-a-syntax.md`) agrees where hygiene and the lambda binding are concerned, disagrees where it substitutes a pattern variable into any term position and where it requires errors at use sites, and is silent on the preparser, on keywords, on statements and on whitespace — that is, on four of the six things that actually cost time here.

## The shape that came out of it

The design the ladder ended with, stated so a later reader can copy it: no function value crosses a rule boundary untyped; a function appears in the sub-language only as a name that resolves at the use site to a typed host declaration, or as a lambda that one rule writes whole; every rule expands to one typed entry of a vocabulary that already exists and is imported unchanged; rank stays in the type; the glue library holds only the patterns the vocabulary does not spell; the names are a closed set, one grammar line each; and the separators are the sub-language's own glyphs, chosen outside the host's operator table.

In numbers: 446 lines of grammar, 197 alternatives of which 124 are name lines and 73 are rules, beside 39 lines and eleven declarations of glue — against the universal base's 899-line grammar and 2,343-line library (`apl/mg/REPORT.md`). What it buys is that the expanded program *is* the target program, so its cost is the target's cost, its numbers are the target's numbers to the last bit, and polishing the vocabulary polishes the notation.

The shape is available to any sub-language whose programs are known in advance. A sub-language meant for programs not yet written pays the universal base's price instead, and the rows above say exactly what that price is.

# Extending Fortress's syntax: lessons from the APL ladder

Between 2026-09-11 and 2026-09-15 an APL was written as a sub-language of Fortress: a feasibility study (`apl-probes/REPORT.md`), six rungs of Stefan Kruger's "Learning APL" climbed chapter by chapter inside `apl⦇ … ⦈` (`apl/rung-1` … `apl/rung-6`), a port of a 25-line flat-style microGPT (`apl/microgpt/`), and then a rewrite of the calling convention for that one program (`apl/mg/`). The purpose was never APL: it was to find where the specification's syntax-extension mechanism and the library give out, and what exactly gives. This document is what a later DSL writer needs in the order they will meet it; the evidence is in the ledger's rows 179-287 and in the probe directories named beside each claim.

The one thing to know before starting: the mechanism runs, it carried a real language, and every wall it has is documented below, but the tooling around it is the worst in the tree, so plan the work as a sequence of small bisecting probes rather than as one grammar you debug at the end.

## Declaring a grammar and importing it

The form that is implemented is FOOL'09's `grammar … end`, declared inside an api; the specification's own normative form, `syntax OpenExpander Id CloseExpander = Expr`, is not implemented at all, and the word `syntax` is not even a declaration keyword (row 267, `apl-probes/b12_spec_syntax_form.fss`). Chapter 27 of the specification is a one-sentence stub pointing at the paper, so the only description of the live spelling in this tree is `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Syntax.rats`, 434 lines; read it first, because most of the shipped examples are written in a dead pre-`=>` spelling that fails to parse, and the build never runs them (row 268 — `SyntaxAbstractionJUTestAll.java:36` and `:39` glob the top directory only, and `build.xml:1260` hangs off `testNightly`, so the green suite says nothing about syntax abstraction either way).

A grammar may live only in an api, never in a component (row 269), so a sub-language is always three files: the grammar api, a stub component exporting it, and the component that uses it (`apl-probes/e30_aplg.fsi` + `e30_aplg.fss` + `e30_apl.fss`, and at scale `apl/base/AplSyntax.fsi` + `AplCore.fss`). They need not sit in one directory, but `FORTRESS_SOURCE_PATH` replaces the shipped default rather than extending it, and the default is four entries (row 190).

Three spellings cost a run each if you do not know them. An api that gives one of its own nonterminals an AST type must `import FortressAst.{...}`, or every annotation in it is undefined, with no diagnostic naming the missing import and nothing in the specification mentioning it (row 271, `gap-ledger-probes/apl-merge/f01_noast*`). A nonterminal may not be named with a word of two or more uppercase letters, because such a word is an operator and not an identifier — `WE` is rejected with a bare `Syntax Error` at the name, and the implementation's rule is looser than the specification's, accepting `AAA` (row 193, `NodeUtil.java:1460-1477`). And the expander's brackets are not privileged: `⦇` U+2987 and `⦈` U+2988 are simply unused anywhere in the parser, the operator table, the library or the specification, so they were free (row 277); any glyph run works that contains none of the macro language's special characters.

The tax is the edit-run loop. Two Rats! parser generations happen at run time, about forty seconds on a cold cache, so a JDK with `javac` on the classpath is a hard requirement for any program that uses a grammar (row 266). `fortress parse` checks the preparser and parser in about 0.6 s and is the only fast check available — but it always fails on a component that *uses* an expander, with an empty message, because it does not run the syntax-abstraction phase (row 191). So grammar apis can be checked quickly and using components cannot, which is why every rung of the ladder kept its probes as separate small components with their own grammars.

## What a gap can and cannot be

A gap is a pattern variable in a production, typed `Id`, `Expr`, or one of your own nonterminals, and it is the only way text from the use site reaches the expansion. An `Expr` gap is the workhorse and behaves well, with one large caveat about greed treated below. The `Id` gap is where the design gives out.

An `Id` gap works in exactly one position: spliced into a lambda parameter, where it binds an ordinary Fortress variable that later statements of the sub-language read under their own spelling and that host code in the same block reads as itself (row 201, `apl/v1-probes/q01_bind.fss`, `q06_block.fss`). It cannot be read as a variable reference anywhere — bare it dies in the template parser, and kept off an expression's first token it dies in the disambiguator, because `Transform.forVarRef` looks a `VarRef`'s id up in the hygiene environment instead of recurring into it, so a gap inside a `VarRef` is never substituted (rows 182, 202). It cannot stand left of `=` or `:=`, because the template parser reads that position with its `AssignLeft` production, where a gap's text arrives null (rows 186, 196); four spellings were tried across two rungs before the design moved. And it refuses `_`, so APL's throw-away name had to be given a real one (row 242).

Repetition works, with one legal use. A `*`- or `+`-bound gap splices into a template with `**`, but only into a list literal carrying an explicit static type — drop the `[\ZZ32\]` and the aggregate's element type is computed from the runtime class and the unification fails (row 272, row 20's mechanism met through an expansion). Used without the `**` splice, the same gap crashes the generated parser with a raw Java cast error and no Fortress diagnostic at all (row 273; `ComposingSyntaxDefTranslator.java:489-490` returns the raw Java list with its conversion commented out beneath). A bound `?` gap — a `Maybe`-typed optional — is `not supported now`, with twenty lines of implementation commented out under the throw (row 274, `:508-509`); that is why an elided axis in `m[1;]` needs a production of its own rather than an optional gap, and why a reduce slash cannot be made optional inside one production (rows 197, 180).

The last constraint is the deepest: a transformer is a template, not a computation. `case … of` in a transformer dispatches only on `Cons(h,t)` and `Empty` over a repetition-bound list, never on an AST constructor name, and asking what an `Expr` gap *is* gives `Unrecognized constructor name: IntLiteralExpr` (row 275; `TemplateVarRewriter.java:122-147` and `Transform.java:752-762`, with `// Nothing else implemented yet`). So the grammar can ask how many items a repetition matched and nothing else. Every decision that depends on a value belongs in the expansion, which is why the feasibility grammar carried each glyph to the expansion as a `String` and let two dispatchers in the using component do the work (row 282), and why the later bases expanded straight to typed calls.

## Hygiene, and the two ways a name can meet its binder

Hygiene is implemented, and it is exactly what forbids the obvious trick. A binder written as a literal identifier inside a template is gensymmed; the free name of another rule's template is not; so the two never meet, and a preamble written by one rule — `(fn (v, m) => (blk))(cell(), cell())` — leaves every reference template unbound (row 204, `apl/v1-probes/q08_cell.fss`, which fails with `Variable m is not defined.` reported at the grammar api's line 1). A name and its binder can therefore meet in only two ways: both come through a gap (row 201), or both come from the use site's own declarations (row 206).

The second of those is the mechanism everything here is built on: free identifiers inside a `<[ … ]>` template resolve at the use site, not in the grammar's api (row 270, `apl-probes/b05_hygiene.fss`). A grammar may name `aplDy`, `rows`, `gather`, `pow`, and the component that uses the grammar supplies them — so a grammar api never has to export an operator across an api boundary, which is the standing workaround for row 30. The host may also simply declare the sub-language's variables, and then both sides see every update across separate use sites (row 206).

The flip side is the error story, and it is bad. An unbound free name in a template is a static failure before anything runs, reported against the grammar api at line 1 column 2 (row 243); so is a type error inside an expansion (row 213); so is a missing overload reached through an expansion, which arrives as a host unification error against the same span (row 230). A use of the expander that matches no production is not reported as a syntax error at all — the bracketed text is left unparsed and the keyword before it is read as an ordinary identifier, `Variable apl is not defined` (row 229). A partial match does at least give a `Syntax Error` at a real column, though the column is the furthest-failure position and not the offending token (rows 242, 261). The paper this mechanism comes from requires errors at use sites to refer to the unexpanded program at use sites; this implementation does the opposite, and the practical consequence is that a sub-language of any size is debugged by bisection.

One positive to end on: a typed lambda written whole inside one template works and dispatches, because hygiene renames the binder and its references together, and the lambda then selects an arrow-typed overload exactly as a hand-written one does (row 285, `apl/probes-4b/y02_lambda.fss`; the negative control, a binder in one template and its reference in another, is `y04_split.fss`). A template can also assign, if the left of `:=` is a literal name of the template rather than a gap (row 205) — so the wall of rows 186 and 196 is the gap, not the assignment.

## The closed name sets, and why

Since a name cannot be read through a gap, a sub-language that wants `v` to mean the user's `v` must spell the name in the grammar: a character class of letters concatenated right-recursively into a `String`, which is how the shipped `Xml.fsi` builds its attribute names (row 194). The class must be letter-then-letter-or-digit, APL's own rule: a single class `[A:Za:z0:9]` is tried before a numeral and the `9` of `9 2 6` is read as a name.

And a terminal that is a valid identifier becomes a keyword of the *whole language*: it is made a `KeywordSymbol`, every keyword of a user grammar is added to `FORTRESS_KEYWORDS`, and `Id` then excludes it, so writing `v` as a terminal to recognise it makes `v` unreadable as a name everywhere, templates included (row 203; the bisection is `q04`/`q05`). Spelled as a character class, `[v]`, it is a `CharacterClassSymbol` and reserves nothing. The same fact prices the entry form: a bare `apl` keyword would reserve the word `apl` program-wide, while `apl⦇` is not a valid identifier and so is an ordinary token.

The consequence is a closed name set: one grammar alternative per name, sixty-five array names, twenty-six strand names and five function names by the last rung of the universal base, and 124 of the focused base's 197 alternatives. It is cheap to write and it has three costs worth knowing in advance. A name outside the set is a `Syntax Error` at the use site rather than a value error at run time. A strand rule over every name merges two names on consecutive lines into one strand, so rung 5 had to read a *third*, disjoint set for strand elements (row 253). And a name may carry a digit after a capital and an underscore, but the underscore's class must be written `` [`_] `` — a bare `[_]` is a Syntax Error at the character — and a name with an underscore must stand above its prefix in the set (row 257).

Names must also survive the host. Its keywords are unusable (`value`, `at`, `type`, `label`, `wrapped` and eighty-odd more, rows 8, 262), every name the using component imports is unusable as a local (`Variable rows is already declared`, row 262), and there is no shadowing anywhere in this language, across five kinds of name (rows 92, 147, 167, 168). On the lambda route a name can also be bound only once per block, since a second `←` is a nested lambda parameter of the same name (row 207). The way out of that one is to bind a *mutable value* rather than to rebind: the library's arrays are mutable through a `Vector`/`Matrix` parameter, so `v[3] ← ¯1` became an in-place put and every later assignment stopped being a rebinding (row 224).

## PEG greed, and where rule order decides

The generated parser is a Rats! PEG: ordered choice, no backtracking into a nonterminal for a shorter match. Every surprise in this section follows from that one sentence.

An undelimited `Expr` gap is greedy and swallows whatever host-known operator follows it: `⍎v ≡ 1 4⍴⍎v` parsed as one `EQV` application inside the first gap (row 183). Delimiters do not help, because the closing delimiter is not a barrier the gap can see: a rule `( a:AplE , b:AplE ) ⍴ r` never matches once the grammar also has a catenate rule, and only atom-typed gaps make it match (row 235). The rule this yields for separators is sharp and was learned twice: a host `Expr` gap may be followed only by a terminal that is *outside* the host's operator table, or by one of your own nonterminals — a rule `y⦇ a:Expr ⋄ b:Expr ⦈` never matches, because `⋄` is the host's DIAMOND operator, and `∘` behaves the same, while `⍤`, which is in no host table, separates cleanly (row 284, `apl/probes-4b/y01_named.fss`).

Inside an ordinary nonterminal, rule order decides: the first alternative that succeeds wins, so a specialised rule must stand above the general one it refines. A rule whose left argument is parenthesised must stand above the plain rule for the same glyph, or the atom rule's own `( … )` consumes the parenthesis first and the specialised rule is never reached — and the failure is not a syntax error but a *wrong parse* that reaches the library and surfaces as a missing overload against the grammar api (row 236). The folded reduction `+/l×r` must likewise stand above the plain `+/v` (row 287).

Between alternatives of one macro *bracket*, order does not decide at all: the closing bracket makes the parser backtrack across alternatives, so a shorter alternative placed above a longer one still lets the longer one match (row 287's positive half). Two more bracket facts cost a worker four false diagnoses between them: a use of the expander cannot be an operand of a juxtaposition — `("" apl⦇ 5 ⦈)` is `Variable apl is not defined`, while the same use as a function argument or a binding's right-hand side parses (row 239) — and nine uses of the expander in one expression do not parse where eight do (row 261).

What the PEG gives for free is worth saying too: APL's strand notation needs ordered choice and nothing else. `AplStrand` is right-recursive over the host's `LiteralExpr` and backtracks at the first glyph, so `2 3 ⍴ ⍳ 6` needs no lookahead predicate; and right-to-left evaluation falls out of the *shape* of the productions — a dyadic rule takes a strand on the left and the whole rest of the expression on the right — so the host's precedence simply does not apply inside the brackets (`apl-probes/REPORT.md` §E, row 282).

## Separators, line breaks and the host's operator table

Whitespace in a production is optional at the use site: a literal space between symbols and an explicit `SPACE` both translate to the host's optional-whitespace nonterminal `w` (row 179). That is what lets a book's examples be copied in verbatim. The converse is that nothing can *require* a space, and `#` after a symbol is the deletion of that optional `w`, not a way to demand one (row 212); its real uses are gluing a name's characters together and gluing a high minus to its digits.

Because `w` crosses line breaks, a line break does not separate two statements whenever the next line can extend the phrase above it. The ladder widened this four times: first by a numeral (row 228), then by any dyadic glyph (row 238), then by the operand of a dfn or a named function (row 241), and finally by two ordinary names (row 253). Three remedies exist, all used: an explicit separator terminal (`⋄`), a comment tail bounded by the end of the line — which needs `#` on *every* symbol of it, or the optional whitespace looks past the newline and the comment swallows the statements below (row 227) — and a non-consuming `AND NEWLINE` lookahead for a form that ends at the line (row 209). A form with no terminator at all parses and then silently runs on (row 210), which is why the shipped regex grammar's bracket-free shape is safe only because a regex is closed by its second slash.

A line break *inside* a production is the opposite of optional whitespace: it is a required line break at the use site, so a rule split across two lines never matches a use written on one, and a long production must be written on one long line however wide (row 244). The break before `=>` is a different position and is free.

Statements are available: `⋄` as an ordinary terminal separates them, and so does a line break written in the production, which becomes the host parser's own `br` — which means a `;` works in its place too (row 208).

The host's operator table is the other half of the design. APL's functional-symbol block U+2336-U+237A is not an operator character set, by specification as well as by implementation: the operator characters are enumerated in `appendices/operators.tex`, and the only U+23xx codepoints there are `⌈ ⌉ ⌊ ⌋`; adding a glyph means regenerating `Operators.java` from `operators.txt`, that is, changing the language (row 278). Inside a sub-grammar the same glyphs are ordinary terminals, and so is any character class over them, because a generated Rats! parser matches raw characters and never goes through the Fortress lexer (row 276). But the *shared* glyphs are usable at the ordinary level and should be: `× ÷ - + * ⊖ ⊂ ⊃ ≡ ≢ ∘` each take a prefix and an infix declaration, so APL's monadic/dyadic split is ordinary overloading (rows 216, 279); `≠ < > ≥ ∧ ∨` take infix declarations returning an array rather than a `Boolean` (rows 218, 233); `⌈ ⌊` are enclosers and can only be declared as bracketing operators with unparenthesised parameters (rows 216, 280); `,` takes neither fixity. So a glyph can be reached two ways, and the ladder used both: a real host operator where the table allows one, a terminal plus a template where it does not.

The macro language's own special characters — `space : ? # + * [ ] | _ { }` and the backtick — must be backtick-escaped in a *terminal*, though not inside a template (row 222), and `\` and `.` refuse the escape entirely, being plain items (row 250). The escape is also this mechanism's nastiest trap. The preparser reads a backtick as an opening quote wanting a closing one and rejects the api — unless an APL glyph stands above it, because the preparser cannot tokenise such a glyph, its token loop then stops, and the delimiter check is silently skipped from there on (row 181). The portable form of the same trick is a `**` above the escape, which is why the shipped `Regex.fsi`, which backtick-escapes nine characters, is accepted at all: it disables the checker on its own line 93 (row 211). Both rows are worth reading before writing a production that needs an escape.

## What a template can and cannot expand to

It can expand to a host operator application, prefix or infix, with the operator characters unescaped (row 222); to a call; to a typed lambda written whole (row 285); to an assignment to a literally named `var` (row 205); to a list literal with a `**` splice, if the literal carries a static type (row 272); and to a block of statements. It cannot expand to a binding or an assignment whose left side is a gap (rows 186, 196), and it cannot mention a name the use site does not have (rows 204, 243).

One silent failure is worth more than the rest of this section. A template that writes the host's caret drops its right operand without a word: `<[ (1.0 (l)) ^ (r) ]>` expands to `1.0 (l)`, so `apl⦇ 10*10 ⦈` evaluated to `10.0` and `apl⦇ 2*3 ⦈` to `2.0`, the causal mask came out `-10` instead of `-1E10`, and every loss of the model moved from the seventh digit — three runs before the cause was found (row 286, `apl/mg/checks/model_run.out.1`). Routed through a one-line glue function `pow(b: RR64, e: ZZ32): RR64 = b^e`, the same rule is exact. Nothing in six rungs had put a host infix operator other than `+ - × ÷` inside a template, which is why nothing caught it earlier. The rule for the next sub-language: no host caret in a template, and treat any other host operator in a template as unproven until a probe prints its value.

## Function values, the frame stack, and why it was replaced

APL's direct functions take implicit arguments `⍺` and `⍵` and recur implicitly through `∇`. None of those can be a binder written by a template, because hygiene renames a template's own binder and the reference written by another rule never meets it (row 204), and the host refuses a nested lambda that re-declares an enclosing name (row 207). So the universal base answered with a frame stack: every APL function value, glyphs included, is a zero-parameter lambda over one mutable stack of frames; `aplCall(f, ⍺, ⍵)` pushes, calls `f()`, and pops; `⍺ ⍵ ∇` are frame reads; and APL's own rule that `⍺ ⍵` are never inherited comes for free (row 245). It is the only shape that survives nesting, and it carried two whole chapters of the book, including dops-in-waiting and glyphs as first-class values (row 234).

It cost three things. Everything on that route is untyped — `() -> Any` in and `Object` out — because an overloaded family whose declared *result* type is `Any` does not dispatch at all, however exactly the parameters match (row 240), leaving `Object` as the only declarable result and one contested row about whether the interpreter should accept a tuple declared that way (row 258). It is slow where the call is per element: 3.5× a direct `+` on scalars and nothing measurable on 100-element vectors (row 245), but 3.8× on a real 16×16 product, which pays 8192 frame pushes (row 256). And it is unsafe under the language's own implicit parallelism: the elements of a tuple expression are evaluated in parallel in separate implicit threads, so `¨` over a strand of three arrays pushed three frames onto one stack and the model died at pool size 4 (row 265). The base sequences the two sites it controls, and the limit stands everywhere else the host may evaluate two calls in parallel.

The focused base dropped the whole mechanism for the one program that mattered. Its single principle is that no function value crosses a rule boundary untyped: a function appears in APL text only as a *name*, which resolves at the use site to a typed host declaration (rows 270, 285) and picks its overload by arrow type (row 171), or as a derived function that one rule expands whole, so hygiene's renaming is consistent within it. That removed the `Any`, the `Object`, the frame pushes and the race together, and the sub-language then cost what the hand-written program costs at both pool sizes (`apl/mg/REPORT.md`). What was given up is real: dfn bodies, `⍺ ⍵ ∇`, guards, dops, glyphs as values — the subject of two of the six rungs.

The lesson generalises. If your sub-language needs user-written functions with implicit arguments, the frame stack is the shape that works; expect it to be untyped, about 3.5× per call, and to need every parallel-evaluated group sequenced by hand. If the programs are known in advance, spend the rules on them instead and keep everything typed.

## Rank in the type

The first APL library carried the rank as run-time data: one `value object AplArr(shape, data)` with every primitive dispatching on a string. It worked, and it was retired after two rungs because it was an interpreter nested inside the interpreter and taught nothing about Fortress (`apl/README.md`; its probes survive as `apl/v1-probes/` because the mechanism rows cite them).

The replacement put the rank in the type: a scalar is an `RR64`, a vector a `Vector[\RR64,s\]`, a matrix a `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]`, a rank-3 array an `Array3` (row 246). That buys a great deal from the host. Rank overloading works and the `nat` is inferred from a runtime-built array (row 214); overloading on the *index's* rank works too, so "a scalar index lowers the rank, a vector index keeps it" is dispatch and never a shape test (row 225); a six-line view object over a runtime-sized matrix is a real `Vector` where the library's own slice is not (rows 226, 55); `requires` contracts on the declarations fire through a macro expansion as catchable violations, so APL's LENGTH, INDEX and DOMAIN ERROR are contracts (rows 220, 231); a library array is already a full generator, with `|v|`, comprehensions, `SUM` and `BIG MAX` and no mix-in at all (row 221); and the shipped `opr DOT` is already APL's inner product in all four rank pairs (row 254).

It costs one declaration per rank combination — thirty-six for one chapter's bracket algebra (row 225) — and it has one hard edge: the single primitive whose result rank is a run-time value, dyadic `⍴` with a computed left argument, cannot be fixed in the grammar, and reinstating it means a sum type over the ranks plus a `typecase` at the head of every primitive, that is, re-entering the whole design through one glyph (row 223). An element type outside the numeric tower is a second edge: a `Char` array cannot join a rank-overloaded family beside an `RR64` one, because `Vector` demands `T extends Number` and the two are both `Rank1` with nothing excluding between them (row 219), so every character primitive is a separate name family.

The trade, stated once: rank in the type buys the host's dispatch, contracts, generators and parallelism; rank as data buys a computed rank and nested values. The programs in this tree wanted the first, and the measurements say the first is also the fast one.

## The cost facts

A direct grammar rule that reaches a typed library entry costs 3.8× less than the same function routed through the general call, measured on the workload these programs are made of: 12.97 s against 49.32 s for 200 products of 16×16 matrices (row 256). That single number is the argument for the direct rules of rungs 1, 3, 5 and 6, and for the focused base as a whole. One frame push is 3.5× a direct `+` on scalars and unmeasurable on 100-element vectors (row 245): the cost appears exactly where the call is per element.

A rule should delegate rather than loop: the shipped `DOT` is 1.46× a hand-written triple loop in the same library (row 256), so `+.×` is one line per rank pair with a contract above it, not a loop.

Parser generation is the fixed tax: two Rats! generations at run time per program, about forty seconds cold (row 266), and no fast check for a component that uses an expander (row 191). Budget for it, keep probes small, and bisect.

The end-to-end number is the one that settles the approach. The focused base expresses 19 of the program's 25 Dyalog lines as APL text over an existing Fortress vocabulary, and its forward pass agrees with the hand-written program intermediate by intermediate to 0.0, its 40 checks pass at both pool sizes with identical values, and its cost is the hand-written program's: 439 s against 528 s and 444 s at pool size 1, 254 s against 263 s at pool size 4 (`apl/mg/REPORT.md`). The universal base's 1.12× and 1.49× on the same checks were the frame stack and its sequential general route. A sub-language's expansion cannot be better than the vocabulary it expands to — and it need not be worse.

## The walls

**Nested arrays.** The flat carrier's wall is the element type: no element can be an array, and a boxed element is a new *representation* rather than a new function, so one trait and two variants replace one carrier and all sixty-five top-level functions are typed in the old one (row 199; the skeleton runs, so the price is measured and not argued). The ladder's answer was to avoid nesting entirely: a strand of arrays became a Fortress tuple, which dispatches on arity, may be an overloaded family's result type, holds values of three different ranks, and binds through a lambda of that many parameters (row 252). A tuple is not an array, so this works only where the nesting is one level and known — which is where it was.

**Implicit arguments.** `⍺ ⍵ ∇` cannot be binders written by a template (rows 204, 207); either a frame stack with everything that implies, or no user-written functions inside the sub-language. There is no third answer in this implementation.

**Characters.** A `Char` array cannot join the rank-overloaded family (row 219), so characters cost a parallel set of names for every primitive; nine of one chapter's examples and the whole of the character material stayed out of scope for this reason. A string literal has no `\u` escape either, so a glyph must stand in the source — which works, the tree being read as UTF-8 (row 200).

**And the diagnostics.** Every static error inside an expansion points at the grammar api's line 1 (rows 213, 230, 243), a use that matches nothing is not reported as a syntax error at all (row 229), and a reported column is a furthest-failure position rather than the offending token (rows 242, 261). No design choice avoids this; only small components and bisection do.

## Where the record is thin, or disagrees with itself

The ledger and the ladder's reports agree about the mechanism, and where they differed the ledger's row carries the correction rather than the report: rung 2b concluded that a sub-language comment may only follow the *last* statement of a block, which is true only of a tail spelled `NOT ⦈ _` and is corrected by row 227; and `apl/base/AplCore.fss`'s own header says a top-level `opr` declared in an api does not reach an importing component, which row 215 falsifies — row 30 is about library generic code failing to see a user operator, not about a user call site. Four APL rows cited the feasibility study's table as though it had been merged before it was; it is now rows 266-283. One count is off in the review that classified the rows: it prices the syntax-extension worklist item at twenty rows and its own list names twenty-one.

Two thin places are worth naming. Nothing in any of this was run on the bytecode-compiler path — every row is the walk interpreter — and the syntax-abstraction tests are not in the green suite at all (row 268), so the suite says nothing about the mechanism either way. And the one contested claim in this area is row 258's type half: a tuple returned as a declared `Object` result, which the specification does not admit and the walk interpreter accepts.

The paper the rows argue with (`research/extracts/growing-a-syntax.md`) agrees where hygiene and the lambda binding are concerned, disagrees where it substitutes a pattern variable into any term position and where it requires errors at use sites, and is silent on the preparser, on keywords, on statements and on whitespace — that is, on four of the six things that actually cost time here.

## The shape that came out of it

The design the ladder ended with, stated so a later reader can copy it: no function value crosses a rule boundary untyped; a function appears in the sub-language only as a name that resolves at the use site to a typed host declaration, or as a lambda that one rule writes whole; every rule expands to one typed entry of a vocabulary that already exists and is imported unchanged; rank stays in the type; the glue library holds only the patterns the vocabulary does not spell; the names are a closed set, one grammar line each; and the separators are the sub-language's own glyphs, chosen outside the host's operator table.

In numbers: 446 lines of grammar, 197 alternatives of which 124 are name lines and 73 are rules, beside 39 lines and eleven declarations of glue — against the universal base's 899-line grammar and 2,343-line library (`apl/mg/REPORT.md`). What it buys is that the expanded program *is* the target program, so its cost is the target's cost, its numbers are the target's numbers to the last bit, and polishing the vocabulary polishes the notation.

The shape is available to any sub-language whose programs are known in advance. A sub-language meant for programs not yet written pays the universal base's price instead, and the rows above say exactly what that price is.
